title: Caesar's coin (Mark 12:13–17)
hook: whose image is on it? give Caesar his, and God what is God's

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was even, the Hebrew for stone. Your line was the rejected stone.

It starts with flattery, thick as honey. Teacher, we know you're honest, you don't care what anyone thinks, you teach God's way truly. The speakers are some Pharisees with some Herodians, a party named for Herod's family; some readers find it an odd pairing. Mark says they were sent to catch him in his words. Then the question: is it lawful to pay the tax to Caesar, or not? It's a neat trap. Say yes, and he sounds like Rome's man. Say no, and he sounds like a rebel, with Herodians standing right there. Neither answer looks safe. So Jesus asks for something small.
screen: `FLATTERY, THICK AS HONEY.` → `AN ODD PAIR, SENT TO CATCH HIM.` → `SHALL WE GIVE, OR NOT?`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, he says: "bring me a penny, that I may see it." The penny was a denarius, a silver coin; in another of Jesus's parables, it's a day's pay for a laborer. He asks them for one, and they bring it, right there in the temple courts. Then the question: "Whose is this image and superscription?" Image and inscription. They answer: "Caesar's." The coin carries the emperor's face and his words. Then the line: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And Mark says they marveled at him. Some readers hear something folded inside it. The same word, image, appears in the Bible's first chapter, where God makes human beings in his own image. So if a coin with Caesar's face belongs to Caesar, give it back to him. And what does Genesis say carries God's image? Every person. Jesus doesn't spell that out; readers hear it. Caesar gets the coin; the person belongs to God. Christians have drawn different practical conclusions from this line. Some hear a clear line between church and state. Others hear a limit on what any government can claim. Others pay their taxes and also say that conscience belongs to God alone. What they share is the picture: a face on a coin, a face in the mirror, and the question of whose each one is.
screen: `BRING ME A PENNY.` · `WHOSE IMAGE IS THIS?` · `GIVE CAESAR WHAT BEARS HIS FACE.` · `YOU BEAR GOD'S IMAGE.` · then, large: `RENDER TO CAESAR THE THINGS THAT ARE CAESAR'S, AND TO GOD THE THINGS THAT ARE GOD'S.`

segments.voice: If you have a coin or a bill nearby, hold it and look at the face on it, or just picture one; then think of your own face, the one the Bible says carries God's image. What in your day belongs to Caesar, the bills and the job and the rules, and what belongs only to God? If you pray, you can offer that part back.
Caesar's coin. A denarius with the emperor's face: give it to Caesar, and give to God what bears God's image.
Your line: you bear god's image. Caesar gets the coin; the person belongs to God. Day two hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Christians often quote "render to Caesar" in discussions of faith, taxes and government, and some teach from Genesis 1:27 that every person bears God's image and so deserves dignity.

original.note: Greek: image, likeness. the root of the English icon. the same word the Greek Bible uses in Genesis 1:27.

what it means: the coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back; you bear God's image, so give yourself to God.
what a scholar hears: eikōn, the coin's image, and the image of Genesis 1:27; the question is less about tax than about what belongs to whom.

chat.says: What did Jesus mean by 'give to Caesar what's Caesar's'?
options: The coin bears Caesar's image, so give it back; people bear God's image.
That faith is only about prayer, so money and rulers don't matter to it.
That paying Rome was forbidden, and he was saying so in secret code.
chat.meaning: The denarius carried Caesar's face. Genesis says people carry God's image: Caesar gets the coin; the person belongs to God.

Genesis.meaning: the Bible's first book, where God makes people in his image

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Removed unsourced history: "Normally these two groups didn't agree", "the crowd, who hate the Roman tax", and the Tiberius coin inscription (teach, myth, trapdoor). "About a day's wage" now rests on Matthew 20:2 (cited). "He doesn't carry it" overclaimed Mark; now "he asks them for one". The narrator's "God asks for the person" recast as what readers hear, since Jesus doesn't say it. "Many Christians" softened; one myth item replaced.

The denarius of Tiberius (inscription TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS) is the usual identification; Mark doesn't name the emperor. Confirm 'many carried words calling him the son of the divine Augustus'.
Genesis 1:27 in the Septuagint uses eikōn; confirm.
Herodians described as 'supporters of Herod's family, which ruled with Rome's blessing'; confirm.
Three church-and-state readings kept general and unranked.
